## How to know der, die, or das — German noun gender rules
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/der-die-das

How to know if a noun is der, die, or das Rules for predicting German noun gender — and what to do when the rules don't apply. Every German noun has a grammatical gender: masculine ( der ), feminine ( die ), or neuter ( das ). Gender controls articles, adjective endings, and pronouns, so guessing wrong changes a lot in one sentence. The honest answer up front: there is no single rule that covers every noun. But about 80% of nouns follow predictable patterns — learn those patterns and you'll guess correctly far more often than by chance. Rule 1: by noun ending Endings are the most reliable shortcut. These are near-universal: Ending Usually Examples -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ik, -ur die (feminine) die Zeitung, die Freiheit, die Universität -e (most) die (feminine) die Lampe, die Blume, die Tasche -chen, -lein das (neuter) das Mädchen, das Büchlein -ment, -tum, -um, -ma das (neuter) das Argument, das Datum, das Thema -er (agent), -ling, -ich, -ig, -ismus der (masculine) der Lehrer, der Frühling, der Tourismus -or, -ist, -ant, -ent der (masculine) der Doktor, der Student, der Tourist Rule 2: by meaning Masculine (der) Male people and animals: der Mann , der Vater , der Hund . Days, months, seasons: der Montag , der Juli , der Winter . Weather, directions, points of the compass: der Regen , der Norden . Alcoholic drinks (with one famous exception, das Bier ): der Wein . Car brands: der BMW , der Audi . Feminine (die) Female people and animals: die Frau , die Mutter , die Katze . Most numbers and ordinals as nouns: die Eins . Most trees and flowers: die Eiche , die Rose . Motorcycle and ship brands: die Harley , die Titanic . Neuter (das) Young creatures: das Kind , das Baby , das Kalb . (Yes, this is why das Mädchen is neuter.) Metals and chemical elements: das Gold , das Eisen . Infinitives used as nouns: das Schwimmen , das Lesen . Most colors and languages as nouns: das Rot , das Deutsch . Rule 3: compound nouns take the last noun's gender Compounds are easy: the final noun decides the article. die Tür + der Schlüssel = der Türschlüssel . If you know the simple noun, you know the compound. What to do when you can't guess When the ending doesn't help and the meaning doesn't fit any category, there's no shortcut — you have to learn the article with the noun. A few habits that work: Always write new vocabulary as article + noun + plural : die Tür, -en , not just Tür . Read the article out loud every time. After a few weeks the wrong article starts sounding wrong. When you read a new sentence and aren't sure about a word's gender, check it — don't let a guess become a habit. Not sure about a specific sentence? Paste it into the Satzbau analyzer and it'll show you every noun's article and plural at once. Related: German plural rules · The four German cases · Accusative vs dative

## Haben or sein in German Perfekt? — rules + list
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/haben-or-sein

Haben or sein as auxiliary? How to choose the right helping verb for the German Perfekt. German uses the perfect tense ( Perfekt ) for almost all spoken past actions. Its formula is simple: auxiliary verb + Partizip II. The only question is whether the auxiliary should be haben or sein . Most verbs take haben . A smaller group takes sein . Default rule: haben Use haben unless the verb meets a specific condition that requires sein . Ich habe ein Buch gelesen. Sie hat Kaffee getrunken. Wir haben im Park gespielt. Use sein if the verb meets any of these Movement from A to B — the subject goes somewhere. Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. Sie ist nach Hause gegangen. Change of state — the subject becomes something different. Der Baum ist gewachsen. Das Kind ist eingeschlafen. Das Eis ist geschmolzen. These three verbs, always: sein (to be), bleiben (to stay), werden (to become). Ich bin müde gewesen. Er ist Arzt geworden. Common sein-verbs to memorize Verb Partizip II Meaning gehen gegangen to go kommen gekommen to come fahren gefahren to drive / travel fliegen geflogen to fly laufen gelaufen to run reisen gereist to travel schwimmen geschwommen to swim springen gesprungen to jump steigen gestiegen to climb / rise sterben gestorben to die wachsen gewachsen to grow aufstehen aufgestanden to get up einschlafen eingeschlafen to fall asleep passieren passiert to happen bleiben geblieben to stay sein gewesen to be werden geworden to become The tricky case: fahren, fliegen, schwimmen Verbs of motion normally take sein , but if you use them transitively — with a direct object — they flip to haben . Ich bin nach Italien geflogen. (I flew to Italy — motion, sein) Der Pilot hat die Maschine geflogen. (The pilot flew the plane — transitive, haben) Sie ist über den See geschwommen. (movement, sein) Sie hat eine neue Technik geschwommen. (transitive, haben — rare but correct) Austrian and Swiss usage In southern German, Austrian, and Swiss usage, sitzen , stehen , and liegen often take sein . In standard northern German, they take haben . Both are accepted. Not sure which auxiliary a verb takes? The Satzbau analyzer shows the auxiliary for every verb in your sentence. Related: Partizip II formation · Strong verb list

## The four German cases explained — nominative, accusative, dative, genitive
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/german-cases

The four German cases explained Nominative, accusative, dative, genitive — what each one does and how to spot it. German marks the role of a noun in a sentence using case. Instead of relying on word order (as English does), German changes the articles and some endings. There are four cases: nominative, accusative, dative, and genitive. Learning them is the single biggest investment that pays off in every German sentence you read or write. Definite article table Case masc fem neut plural Nominative der die das die Accusative den die das die Dative dem der dem den (+n) Genitive des (+s) der des (+s) der Nominative — the subject The nominative is the "who is doing the action" case. It's the form you find in a dictionary. Der Hund schläft. — the dog is the subject. Also used after sein , werden , bleiben : Das ist ein Student . Accusative — the direct object The accusative marks the thing being directly acted on. Ich sehe den Mann. — den Mann is what I see. Always after these prepositions: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um . After two-way prepositions when there's motion toward a destination. Dative — the indirect object The dative marks the recipient — "to whom" or "for whom" something happens. Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel. — dem Kind is the recipient. Always after these prepositions: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber . After two-way prepositions when describing static location. With dative-only verbs: helfen, danken, folgen, gefallen, gehören, antworten , etc. Plural nouns add an -n in dative if they don't already end in -n or -s : mit den Kindern . Genitive — possession and formal prepositions Genitive expresses possession or relationship. It's slightly formal; spoken German often replaces it with von + dative. Das Auto meines Vaters. — my father's car. Masculine and neuter singular nouns add -s or -es : des Mannes , des Hauses . Genitive prepositions: (an)statt, trotz, während, wegen, außerhalb, innerhalb . In conversation, wegen dem Regen is common (dative); in writing, wegen des Regens is standard. How to identify a case in a sentence Find the verb. Is it a dative-only verb? If yes, its object is dative. Find a preposition. If it's in a fixed accusative or dative list, the case is decided. Otherwise, ask wer?/was? → nominative. wen?/was? → accusative. wem? → dative. Paste a sentence into the Satzbau analyzer to see each phrase labeled with its case. Related: Accusative vs dative in detail · Two-way prepositions · der/die/das rules

## Accusative vs dative in German — simple guide with examples
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/accusative-vs-dative

Accusative vs dative in German The core idea, the article endings, the verbs that break the pattern, and worked examples. The core idea in one line Accusative = the direct object (the thing being acted on). Dative = the indirect object (the recipient / the one affected). English uses word order for this. German uses case. Compare: I give the man the book. → Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch. dem Mann = dative (the recipient). das Buch = accusative (the thing given). Ask two questions: Wen/was? (Whom/what [is acted on]?) → accusative. Wem? (To/for whom?) → dative. Article endings — the thing to memorize Case masc fem neut plural Nominative der die das die Accusative den die das die Dative dem der dem den (+n on noun) Notice the shortcut: only the masculine noun changes in accusative ( der → den ). The dative changes everything. That's why masculine nouns are where most learners get stuck first. Indefinite articles follow the same pattern: ein/eine/ein → einen/eine/ein (acc) and einem/einer/einem (dat). Verbs that force dative Some verbs always take a dative object even though English treats them as direct. Memorize these — they're the most common cause of mistakes: helfen — Ich helfe dir. (not dich) danken — Ich danke dem Lehrer. antworten — Sie antwortet mir. folgen — Der Hund folgt dem Mann. gefallen — Das Buch gefällt mir. gehören — Das Auto gehört meinem Bruder. glauben (to a person) — Ich glaube dir. passen , schmecken , fehlen , begegnen Prepositions fix the case Some prepositions always take accusative ( durch, für, gegen, ohne, um ), some always dative ( aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu ), and the two-way prepositions ( in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen ) switch based on motion vs location. See the two-way prepositions guide . Motion vs location test Ich gehe in die Schule. (motion → accusative) Ich bin in der Schule. (location → dative) Worked examples Er gibt seiner Schwester einen Brief. — seiner Schwester dative (recipient), einen Brief accusative (object given). Sie hilft dem alten Mann. — dative because helfen is a dative verb. Wir legen das Buch auf den Tisch. — accusative because there's motion onto the table. Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. — dative because it's a static location. See the case of every phrase in your own sentences: paste them into the Satzbau analyzer . Related: All four German cases · Two-way prepositions · der/die/das rules

## German two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen) — accusative vs dative
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/two-way-prepositions

German two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen) Nine prepositions that can take accusative or dative. Here's how to pick the right one. German has nine "two-way" prepositions — called Wechselpräpositionen — that can govern either the accusative or the dative case. The choice depends on whether the verb describes motion toward a new location (accusative) or a static location or motion within a space (dative). The nine Wechselpräpositionen Preposition Meaning in in, into an at, on (vertical surface), to auf on (horizontal surface), onto über over, above, across unter under, below vor in front of, before hinter behind neben next to, beside zwischen between The rule: Wohin? vs. Wo? Ask a test question: Wohin? (Where to?) → motion into a new place → accusative . Wo? (Where?) → static position or motion within a fixed area → dative . Side-by-side examples Accusative (Wohin?) Dative (Wo?) Ich gehe in die Küche. Ich bin in der Küche. Sie hängt das Bild an die Wand. Das Bild hängt an der Wand. Er legt das Buch auf den Tisch. Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. Der Vogel fliegt über den Fluss. Die Lampe hängt über dem Tisch. Die Katze kriecht unter das Bett. Die Katze schläft unter dem Bett. Ich stelle das Fahrrad vor das Haus. Das Fahrrad steht vor dem Haus. Er geht hinter das Gebäude. Er wartet hinter dem Gebäude. Sie setzt sich neben ihn . Sie sitzt neben ihm . Er stellt die Vase zwischen die Bücher. Die Vase steht zwischen den Büchern. Two very useful verb pairs German distinguishes placement (accusative, motion) from position (dative, state). These pairs come up all the time: stellen (to put, upright) vs. stehen (to stand) legen (to put, lying) vs. liegen (to lie) setzen (to set/sit down) vs. sitzen (to sit) hängen (to hang — transitive/accusative) vs. hängen (to hang — intransitive/dative) If the verb is from the left column (placement), you're heading into a new position → accusative. Right column verbs describe state → dative. Common contractions in das → ins — ich gehe ins Kino in dem → im — ich bin im Kino an das → ans an dem → am auf das → aufs (informal) When motion verbs still take dative Watch out: a verb of motion that describes movement within a place (not toward a new one) takes dative. Ich laufe im Park. (I run around inside the park — dative) Ich laufe in den Park. (I'm running into the park from outside — accusative) Second-guessing a case? Paste the sentence into the Satzbau analyzer and each phrase gets labeled with its case and role. Related: Accusative vs dative · The four German cases

## Partizip II in German — how to form it + common list
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/partizip-2

Partizip II: how to form the German past participle Rules for weak, strong, and mixed verbs, plus a list of common irregulars. Partizip II (the past participle) is what you need to build the perfect tense ( Perfekt ), the pluperfect ( Plusquamperfekt ), the passive, and many adjectives. Most German conversations about the past use Perfekt, so this form is everywhere. Weak verbs — regular pattern Weak verbs (the vast majority) form Partizip II with ge- + stem + -t . machen → gemacht lernen → gelernt kaufen → gekauft arbeiten → gearbeitet (stems ending in -t, -d add -et) Strong verbs — vowel change + -en Strong verbs change their stem vowel and end in -en . singen → gesungen schreiben → geschrieben fahren → gefahren gehen → gegangen There's no shortcut — you memorize strong verbs one by one. See the strong verb list . Mixed verbs — vowel change + -t A small group mixes both: stem change plus -t ending. bringen → gebracht denken → gedacht kennen → gekannt wissen → gewusst When the "ge-" prefix is dropped Two rules cancel the ge- : Verbs ending in -ieren: studieren → studiert , telefonieren → telefoniert . Verbs with inseparable prefixes (be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver-, zer-, miss-): bekommen → bekommen , verstehen → verstanden , erzählen → erzählt . Separable-prefix verbs With separable prefixes, ge- goes between the prefix and the stem. aufmachen → aufgemacht ankommen → angekommen einkaufen → eingekauft Common irregular Partizip II forms Infinitive Partizip II Auxiliary sein gewesen sein haben gehabt haben werden geworden sein gehen gegangen sein kommen gekommen sein fahren gefahren sein essen gegessen haben trinken getrunken haben sehen gesehen haben lesen gelesen haben schreiben geschrieben haben sprechen gesprochen haben nehmen genommen haben finden gefunden haben geben gegeben haben bleiben geblieben sein stehen gestanden haben verstehen verstanden haben bringen gebracht haben denken gedacht haben Not sure about a verb? Paste the sentence into the Satzbau analyzer and it'll show the Partizip II and auxiliary for every verb. Related: Haben or sein? · Strong verb list

## German plural rules — five endings and how to predict them
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/german-plurals

German plural rules Five endings, five patterns. Plus how to predict which noun uses which. German has five main plural endings: -n/-en , -e , -er , -s , and no ending at all. Some also add an umlaut ( ä, ö, ü ) on the stem vowel. There's no single rule, but noun gender and ending make most plurals predictable. In the plural, every article is die , regardless of the singular gender. The five endings at a glance Ending Typical nouns Examples -n / -en most feminine nouns die Frau → Frauen, die Blume → Blumen, die Zeitung → Zeitungen -e (± umlaut) many masculine and some neuter der Tag → Tage, der Stuhl → Stühle, das Jahr → Jahre -er (+ umlaut if possible) many one-syllable neuter nouns das Kind → Kinder, das Haus → Häuser, das Buch → Bücher -s foreign/loan words, words ending in a vowel das Auto → Autos, das Hotel → Hotels, der Park → Parks no ending (± umlaut) masc/neut ending in -er, -en, -el, -chen, -lein der Lehrer → Lehrer, der Vater → Väter, das Mädchen → Mädchen Patterns by gender Feminine nouns ~90% take -(e)n . Almost automatic. die Lampe → Lampen, die Tasche → Taschen, die Universität → Universitäten Exceptions with umlaut + -e: die Hand → Hände, die Stadt → Städte, die Maus → Mäuse . Masculine nouns Most take -e , often with umlaut. der Hund → Hunde, der Zug → Züge, der Arzt → Ärzte Those ending in -er, -en, -el usually take no ending (maybe umlaut): der Bruder → Brüder, der Wagen → Wagen, der Apfel → Äpfel . "Weak" masculines add -(e)n : der Junge → Jungen, der Student → Studenten . Neuter nouns No single rule, but: One-syllable neuter nouns often take -er with umlaut: das Kind → Kinder, das Buch → Bücher . Neuter nouns ending in -chen or -lein never change: das Mädchen → Mädchen . Loan words take -s : das Auto → Autos . Dative plural rule In the dative plural, the noun adds an -n if it doesn't already end in -n or -s . die Kinder → mit den Kindern die Bücher → in den Büchern die Autos → mit den Autos (no change, ends in -s) Learn the plural with the noun The best habit is to learn every new noun with its article and its plural: die Hand, die Hände . Writing vocabulary as three items (article, noun, plural) means you never have to reconstruct the plural from guesses. Want to see the plural of every noun in a sentence at once? Paste it into the Satzbau analyzer . Related: der/die/das rules · German cases

## German word order (Satzbau) — V2, subordinate clauses, TeKaMoLo
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/german-word-order

German word order (Satzbau) The three rules that cover 95% of German sentences. German word order feels unpredictable at first, but it's governed by a small number of rules. The most important one is that the conjugated verb must be the second element in a main clause — almost always. Once you internalize this, German sentences start clicking into place. Rule 1: V2 — the verb is always second in a main clause The conjugated verb occupies the second "position" (not necessarily the second word — the second unit ). Ich gehe heute ins Kino. (Ich / gehe / heute / ins Kino) Heute gehe ich ins Kino. (Heute / gehe / ich / ins Kino) Ins Kino gehe ich heute. (Ins Kino / gehe / ich / heute) The fronted element changes emphasis but the verb stays in position 2. You can move anything to the front, but the verb won't budge. Rule 2: subordinate clauses send the verb to the end After subordinating conjunctions like weil, dass, wenn, obwohl, als, während, damit, ob , the conjugated verb goes to the very end. Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin . Ich weiß, dass du Recht hast . Wenn es regnet, nehme ich einen Regenschirm . (wenn-clause first → main clause starts with the verb to keep V2 globally) Rule 3: in Perfekt/modal/future, the non-finite verb goes to the end When the sentence has more than one verb (auxiliary + participle, or modal + infinitive), the conjugated verb is in position 2 and the other verb goes to the end. Ich habe gestern ein Buch gelesen . Er will morgen nach Berlin fahren . Wir werden nächste Woche unseren Freund besuchen . This is called the Satzklammer (sentence bracket): the verbs form a frame around the rest of the clause. TeKaMoLo — the order of adverbial info When a sentence has several adverbials (time, cause, manner, place), German tends to put them in this order: Te mporal (when?) Ka usal (why?) Mo dal (how?) Lo kal (where?) Example: Ich fahre morgen (Te) wegen der Arbeit (Ka) mit dem Zug (Mo) nach München (Lo). You can front one of these elements to emphasize it (then the verb still comes next, per V2), but their internal order stays TeKaMoLo. Object order: dative before accusative (usually) When both objects are nouns, dative comes first: Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel . When one is a pronoun, the pronoun comes first: Ich gebe ihn (acc) dem Kind (dat). Yes/no questions and commands In yes/no questions and imperatives, the verb is in position 1: Kommst du mit? Geh nach Hause! Want to see how a complex German sentence is structured? Paste it into the Satzbau analyzer and every phrase gets labeled with its role. Related: German cases · Modal verbs

## German modal verbs — können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/modal-verbs

German modal verbs Six verbs that change the meaning of another verb — ability, obligation, permission, desire. German has six modal verbs: können, müssen, dürfen, sollen, wollen, mögen . They work alongside another verb (the infinitive) to express a mode — whether something is possible, required, allowed, expected, wanted, or liked. They're among the most common verbs in spoken German. Meaning in one line each können — can, to be able to müssen — must, to have to dürfen — to be allowed to sollen — should, supposed to wollen — to want to mögen — to like (often used in its subjunctive form möchten = "would like") Present tense conjugation Modals have irregular singular forms (vowel change) but regular plural. können müssen dürfen sollen wollen mögen ich kann muss darf soll will mag du kannst musst darfst sollst willst magst er/sie/es kann muss darf soll will mag wir können müssen dürfen sollen wollen mögen ihr könnt müsst dürft sollt wollt mögt sie/Sie können müssen dürfen sollen wollen mögen Sentence structure The modal is the conjugated verb (position 2 in a main clause); the second verb goes to the end as an infinitive. Ich kann Deutsch sprechen . Du musst jetzt gehen . Wir wollen morgen nach Berlin fahren . Möchten vs. wollen Möchten is the subjunctive of mögen and means "would like" — politer than wollen . In restaurants, shops, or polite requests, use möchten . Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. (polite) Ich will einen Kaffee. (blunt, more like a demand) Past tense: Präteritum is preferred With modals, spoken German usually uses Präteritum , not Perfekt . Ich konnte gestern nicht kommen. (rather than habe nicht kommen können ) Sie musste früh aufstehen. Wir wollten ins Kino gehen. Common meanings in context Das kann sein. — That could be. (possibility) Er muss krank sein. — He must be sick. (logical deduction) Du darfst nicht rauchen. — You're not allowed to smoke. Er soll sehr klug sein. — He's said to be very clever. Ich mag Schokolade. — I like chocolate. (no second verb needed) Curious about how a modal reshapes a sentence? Paste it into the Satzbau analyzer for the full structural breakdown. Related: German word order · Strong verbs

## German strong & irregular verbs — full list with stems
URL: https://satzbau.eu/guides/strong-verbs

German strong & irregular verbs The most common irregular verbs, grouped by vowel pattern. German strong verbs change their stem vowel in the past tense and often in the du/er/sie/es present form too. There's no rule that tells you which vowel change applies — you memorize them. The good news: there are groups, and about 200 strong verbs cover almost everything you'll encounter. Below are the most frequent ones. The essential 60 Infinitive er/sie/es Präteritum (ich) Partizip II Aux Meaning sein ist war gewesen sein to be haben hat hatte gehabt haben to have werden wird wurde geworden sein to become gehen geht ging gegangen sein to go kommen kommt kam gekommen sein to come fahren fährt fuhr gefahren sein/haben to drive laufen läuft lief gelaufen sein to run fliegen fliegt flog geflogen sein/haben to fly to bring (mixed) denken denkt dachte gedacht haben to think (mixed) kennen kennt kannte gekannt haben to know (person) (mixed) wissen weiß wusste gewusst haben to know (fact) (mixed) nennen nennt nannte genannt haben to name (mixed) rennen rennt rannte gerannt sein to run (mixed) brennen brennt brannte gebrannt haben to burn (mixed) Vowel-change patterns Many strong verbs fall into predictable groups. Some of the bigger ones: ei → ie → ie : bleiben–blieb–geblieben, schreiben–schrieb–geschrieben, steigen–stieg–gestiegen. ie → o → o : fliegen–flog–geflogen, verlieren–verlor–verloren, schließen–schloss–geschlossen. i → a → u : singen–sang–gesungen, trinken–trank–getrunken, finden–fand–gefunden. e → a → o : sprechen–sprach–gesprochen, helfen–half–geholfen, nehmen–nahm–genommen. e → a → e : essen–aß–gegessen, geben–gab–gegeben, lesen–las–gelesen. Need the full forms for a specific verb in a sentence? Drop the sentence into the Satzbau analyzer . Related: Partizip II formation · Haben or sein?
